figure: Figure 8.1 (Where inference computation and data movement actually live)
issue: The figure encodes all seven components (registers, tensor cores/ALU, shared mem/SRAM, L2 cache, HBM, GPU interconnect, other GPUs/remote) as one uniform single-column stack with equal vertical gaps and a single red gradient arrow, i.e. visually as ONE ladder. This contradicts the caption's explicit, bolded claim that 'compute, memory and interconnect are separate groups in this figure, not levels of one ladder.' The blue compute box (tensor cores/ALU) is embedded as the 2nd rung inside the column, and the red arrow's vertical span is ambiguous (it does not cleanly bound the memory sub-stack), so a reader who looks at the figure without the caption will form the wrong mental model that the interconnect is merely the 'farthest/slowest rung' of the same speed-capacity-distance gradient and that tensor cores are a memory level. Per the figure-causality standard, the diagram currently requires the caption to be read correctly.
evidence: Rendered page 161: seven same-width boxes stacked with uniform spacing; the red double-headed arrow labeled 'capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows' runs down the right side across the middle of the column; the blue 'tensor cores / ALU' box sits between 'registers' and 'shared mem (SRAM)'. The only disambiguators of the three groups are color (blue/orange/green) and the caption text. Caption (same page) states: 'compute, memory and interconnect are separate groups in this figure, not levels of one ladder - the colors mark the groups, and only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder.'
acceptance_test: After the fix, with the caption hidden, a test reader viewing only the figure must be able to (a) identify three visually distinct groups (compute / memory / interconnect) using structure, not color alone (e.g. group brackets or left-side group labels and a clear vertical gap between the memory sub-stack and the interconnect group); (b) see the red gradient arrow bounded to the memory sub-stack (registers through HBM) only, with unambiguous start and end; and (c) not read the tensor cores/ALU box or the interconnect boxes as rungs of that gradient. Pass = the reader names the three groups and the arrow's extent correctly without the caption.

issue: Each of the three orange GPU boxes in panel B contains an unexplained white rectangle on its left edge and another on its right edge (the red P2P arrows appear to attach to these white boxes). These internal white elements are not defined anywhere: the in-figure legend lists only weights (blue), GPU (orange), data (green), comms (red); the caption ('Each panel names what splits and what communicates') and the grayscale figure note make no mention of them. They are also inconsistent with panels A and C, where the GPU boxes are rendered as solid orange cross-hatched rectangles with no internal white sub-rectangles. A reader cannot tell whether the white boxes mark stage input/output activation buffers, two sub-stages, or the idle-bubble region, which undermines the figure's goal of being immediately interpretable.
evidence: Legend row reads: 'weights (blue) / GPU (orange) / data (green) / comms (red)' — no entry for the white boxes. Caption: 'pipeline parallel splits the layer stack into stages with an idle bubble at fill/drain' — the bubble is described in the text line below the diagram ('idle (bubble) at fill/drain — pipeline-wide'), not tied to the white boxes. Visual comparison: panel A GPU 0/GPU 1 and panel C GPU 0/GPU 1 are uniform orange hatched boxes; only panel B's GPU 0/GPU 1/GPU 2 (layers 1-8 / 9-16 / 17-24) show the left+right white rectangles.
acceptance_test: Either (a) label the white boxes (e.g., small 'in'/'out' tags) and add one clause to the caption such as 'white boxes mark each stage's input/output activation at the P2P boundary', or (b) delete the white boxes and draw the red P2P arrows directly between the GPU box edges so panel B's GPU rendering matches panels A and C. After the fix, a grayscale reader must be able to state what the internal elements (if any remain) represent without guessing, and the three panels must use a consistent GPU-box convention.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3 'Worked Example' — 'Occupancy thresholds' paragraph (after the 'Canonical host verdict' bullet)
quoted_clause: At the canonical operating point the 5.2 ms weight read is not HBM-saturating; it saturates HBM above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) only in the batch-1-equivalent case where each sequence streams its own full 17.5 GB shard, with no weight-read amortization.
observed: As written, the first clause is false for the canonical host. The 5.2 ms figure IS the time to stream the 17.5 GB shard at peak HBM bandwidth: 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.22 ms, i.e. 100% of peak. The sentence appears to intend 'the weight read does not saturate HBM for the whole 25 ms step', but the literal reading tells the reader that a single sequence leaves the memory system idle — the opposite of the truth, and the opposite of the decode-bandwidth-bound verdict the same chapter establishes.
evidence: Recomputed: 17.5e9 B / 3.35e12 B/s = 5.224 ms (matches the book's 5.2 ms). The ~5-seq/GPU threshold is separately correct under a 25 ms-budget reading: B x 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 3.35 TB/s at B = 4.79 ~ 5; and 5 x 8 = 40 per host. So the numbers are right; the sentence that frames them is wrong.
root_cause: Two different framings (bandwidth saturation vs. latency-budget occupancy) are compressed into one clause, and 'batch-1-equivalent' is reused for a second, incompatible meaning (single-request whole-model streaming in §3 vs. a hypothetical multi-sequence no-amortization case here).
correction: Rewrite as two explicit statements: (a) 'At batch 1 the 17.5 GB shard read takes 5.2 ms at peak HBM bandwidth — i.e. the weight read alone saturates HBM for 5.2 ms of the 25 ms step, so the step is bandwidth-bound, not idle.' (b) 'Under a no-amortization model in which each of B sequences independently streams the full shard, the aggregate demand reaches the 3.35 TB/s ceiling at B ~ 4.8 sequences per GPU (~40 per host) within the 25 ms budget; no production engine behaves this way (a real engine reads the shard once per step for the whole batch), so this is an upper bound, not an operating point.' Rename the second case (e.g. 'no-amortization upper bound') so it does not collide with 'batch-1-equivalent'.
acceptance_test: A reader who computes 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s from the text reaches 5.2 ms and finds the sentence consistent with their own arithmetic; the two batching models are named distinctly and each threshold is traceable to one of them.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — Table 2-1, row 'Decode: bandwidth verdict'; and the 'Decode bandwidth' bullet of 'Worked example arithmetic details'
quoted_clause: | Decode: bandwidth verdict | bandwidth-bound | 5.6 > 3.35 → under the batch-1-equivalent model, a single H100 cannot meet the demand; batching/amortization change this (see later chapters) [canonical scenario][DERIVED] |
observed: The row labelled 'bandwidth verdict' (a regime classification) is derived from a capacity comparison (5.6 TB/s demand > 3.35 TB/s peak). The book's own Fig 2.2 caption explicitly separates the two: 'The regime classification and the capacity shortfall are independent'. The prefill row of the same table does it correctly, deriving the regime from arithmetic intensity (~9.2K FLOP/byte > ridge ~295). The decode row therefore mixes the two verdicts the book insists on keeping apart, and a reader can conclude that 'bandwidth-bound' here means 'does not fit on one GPU' rather than 'sits left of the roofline ridge'.
evidence: Decode arithmetic intensity recomputed: per decode step per GPU, weight-matmul FLOPs = 2 x 8.75e9 = 17.5 GFLOP against 17.5 GB of shard reads = 1 FLOP/byte, versus the H100 ridge 989e12/3.35e12 = 295 FLOP/byte. The regime verdict is therefore derivable and is ~1 FLOP/byte, exactly as Fig 2.2 states. The capacity verdict (5.6 > 3.35) is a separate, also-correct statement.
root_cause: The table row was written to carry the capacity conclusion and was given a regime label; the two axes were not separated when the row was authored.
correction: Split the row into two: 'Decode: regime verdict | bandwidth-bound | arithmetic intensity ~1 FLOP/byte (2 x 8.75e9 FLOP per step / 17.5 GB shard read) << ridge ~295 → memory-bound side [canonical scenario][DERIVED]' and 'Decode: single-device capacity verdict | one H100 insufficient | 5.6 TB/s aggregate demand > 3.35 TB/s peak under the batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'. Apply the same split in the 'Decode bandwidth' bullet, where 'the decode phase is HBM-bandwidth-bound' currently follows from '5.6 > 3.35'.
acceptance_test: Every regime verdict in Table 2-1 and in the surrounding prose is justified by an arithmetic-intensity comparison against the ~295 ridge; every capacity verdict is justified by a demand-vs-peak comparison; no sentence uses one to support the other.

page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Concept' — 'Attention' subsection, paragraph introducing the three-row attention-architecture taxonomy table
quoted_clause: The canonical three-row taxonomy, used by name in Ch. 3, Ch. 7 and Appendix A rather than re-described there: [...] This is why "the KV problem" and its fixes are really a *model-architecture* question (Ch. 3) that lands as a *memory* question (Ch. 7) — and why the token layer is the right place to have met it. We only need the concept here; the mechanism inventory is Chapter 3's, the arithmetic Chapter 7's.
observed: Ch 1 defers the GQA/MQA/MLA mechanism inventory to Ch 3, but Ch 3 as written does not deliver it. Ch 3's Concept section is about parameter allocation (dense vs MoE) plus the alternative-inference aside; GQA, MQA and MLA appear only in passing inside the KV discussion of §3 ('MLA-style latent attention does not stop the growth: it cuts the bytes/token constant (~50–60x for DeepSeek-class geometry)'). There is no attention-architecture section, no head-sharing mechanism, no latent-compression mechanism, and no explanation of why GQA/MQA reduce bytes while MLA changes the stored representation. The reader is told a promised mechanism inventory is coming and it never arrives in the chunk.
evidence: Read Ch 3 in full: §1 Concept (parameter allocation regime; alternative-inference aside), §2 Mental Model (resource pool), §3 Worked Example (dense vs MoE arithmetic; 'Why MoE saves compute but not KV cache memory'), §4 Measurement, §5 Common Mistakes, §6 Architecture Consequence, §7 What We Still Don't Know, §8 Mini-Case. No attention-architecture treatment.
root_cause: Ch 1 was written as a concept chapter that names the taxonomy and delegates; the delegate chapter was scoped around parameter allocation and never absorbed the attention-architecture material.
correction: Either (a) add a Ch 3 subsection 'Attention architecture and the KV constant' that gives the mechanism inventory Ch 1 promises — head sharing (GQA/MQA: one KV head serving G query heads; bytes/token scales as 1/G), latent compression (MLA: store the compressed latent d_c plus the decoupled rope part d_h^R instead of per-head K/V), and constant-state recurrent layers (Mamba/linear attention: fixed-size state, no per-token term) — with the byte formulas and one worked geometry each; or (b) rewrite Ch 1's deferral to point at Ch 7 (where the arithmetic lives) and at Appendix A, and drop the claim that Ch 3 holds the mechanism inventory. Option (a) is preferable: Ch 3's own §3 already needs the GQA/MQA/MLA distinction to justify the 'shape, not routing' argument.
acceptance_test: A reader who has read Ch 1 and Ch 3 can explain, in mechanism terms and without consulting Ch 7, why GQA/MQA shrink bytes/token, why MLA shrinks them by a different mechanism, and why neither stops linear growth; and no chapter promises a 'mechanism inventory' that another chapter does not contain.

page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — 'Canonical Workload — the single reference set' box, immediately followed by 'Table 4-2 — Canonical-scenario provenance ledger'
quoted_clause: > **Canonical Workload — the single reference set.** This box is the one authoritative set of numbers every chapter disciplines on. [...] #### Table 4-2 — Canonical-scenario provenance ledger (which value is assumed, derived, or factual) [...] Every quantity below is either an assumed workload input, a vendor fact, a modeled result, or a dated price snapshot. This is the authority for which is which; chapters refer back to it rather than restating provenance each time.
observed: The canonical box and Table 4-2 are two artifacts carrying the same values, and the box is described as 'the one authoritative set' while Table 4-2 is described as 'the authority for which is which'. Thirteen of Table 4-2's eighteen rows duplicate box rows: registered users 2,000; traffic 10/40 rps; execution occupancy ~86/~344; input 9,200; output 300; model 70B; KV per token 2.62 MB; H100 80 GB; H100 0.989 PFLOPS; retrieval 120 ms; prefill budget 1.08 s; TPOT 25 ms; host price ~$20/hr. This is redundant repetition (class C) with a real maintenance hazard: two places to update for every canonical change, and a reader who finds a value in one and not the other cannot tell which is canonical.
evidence: Row-by-row comparison of the box (21 rows) against Table 4-2 (18 rows) in the chunk; 13 values appear in both with identical numbers.
root_cause: The box was introduced for readability and the ledger for provenance, but the ledger was built as a full restatement rather than as a provenance column keyed to the box.
correction: Merge them: give the canonical box a third column ('Status') carrying the provenance/epistemic pair for each row, and delete Table 4-2. Keep Note 1 (the axis definitions) as the single place the taxonomy is defined, and keep the assumption-change log. If the ledger must survive as a separate artifact for citation stability, reduce it to the rows the box does not carry (attention architecture, KV per token FP8, H100 BF16 peak, prefill-budget derivation) and add a line to the box pointing to it.
acceptance_test: Each canonical value appears exactly once in Ch 4's front-of-chapter material; a reader can find the provenance of any canonical number without leaving the artifact that states the number; a change to any canonical value requires editing one place.

page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — canonical box rows 'Availability' and 'Operational constraints'; Table 4-1 'Operational constraints' row; 'Availability topology — UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED' note; §6 'Operational topology' bullet
quoted_clause: | Availability | 99.9% | [...] **Availability topology — UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED in the canonical cost arithmetic.** [...] The canonical cost figures (Ch 16 `$/1K req`, Ch 17 host counts) therefore **understate the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement**.
observed: Two distinct availability gaps are flagged but neither is closed. (a) Topology: the canonical workload requires multi-region active-active; the fleet arithmetic prices single-region N−1. The book is honest that this is unpriced, but the canonical box — the artifact every chapter 'disciplines on' — still asserts multi-region active-active as the workload's operational constraint, so the canonical reference set is internally inconsistent with the canonical fleet design. (b) Arithmetic: nothing in the chunk shows that the priced design (N−1 single-host failover over a 9-host average / 32-host peak fleet) delivers the asserted 99.9% SLA. N−1 over 9 hosts protects against one host failure and leaves 8/9 capacity; it says nothing about zone, power, network, or software failure, and the book never states the failure-domain budget that turns '99.9%' into a design requirement. A reader could reasonably conclude that the canonical fleet meets the canonical SLA, which the book has not established.
evidence: The canonical box's Availability row states 99.9%; the availability-topology note states the TCO/fleet arithmetic prices single-region N−1 and 'understate[s] the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement'; §6 repeats 'UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED'. No availability arithmetic (failure-domain budget, error-budget allocation, MTBF/MTTR inputs) appears anywhere in the chunk.
root_cause: The availability requirement was introduced as a workload input in the six-dimension framework but never converted into a priced design requirement; the book chose to flag the gap rather than close it, and the flag lives in notes rather than in the canonical reference itself.
correction: Two concrete moves. (1) In the canonical box, change the Availability row to state the requirement in the terms the book actually prices — e.g. '99.9% monthly availability, single-region multi-AZ, N−1 host redundancy (multi-region active-active priced separately, see Ch 16–17)' — so the canonical set is self-consistent; keep the multi-region variant as an explicitly unpriced variant. (2) Add a short availability-arithmetic note (Ch 16 or 17): allocate the 99.9% error budget across failure domains (host, zone, region, software), state which domains the N−1 design covers and which it does not, and show the residual budget the design must still satisfy. If the multi-region variant is retained as the canonical requirement, price it (a second capacity line) rather than leaving the canonical workload's own requirement uncosted.
acceptance_test: The canonical reference set contains no requirement that the book's own fleet design does not meet or explicitly price; a reader can state which failure domains the canonical fleet design covers, which it does not, and what error budget remains; the words 'UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED' appear only against variants that are explicitly labelled as variants.

page_hint: Ch 3 §7 'What We Still Don't Know' — first bullet
quoted_clause: - **Exact active-fraction per token for commercial MoE models.** Model cards rarely publish the precise top-k routing distribution under real workloads. We know the architectural top-k (e.g., top-2 from 8 experts), but which experts are active varies with prompt content and token position; *the number* of active parameters per token is fixed by top-k and expert size under standard routing. Effective active count can vary only under variable-k, capacity dropping, or expert-unavailable fallback — an implementation-specific exception, not the default.
observed: The bullet is filed as an open question under [UNRESOLVED], but its own body resolves it: 'the number of active parameters per token is fixed by top-k and expert size under standard routing'. The genuinely open residue is narrow and implementation-specific (variable-k, capacity dropping, expert-unavailable fallback). As written, the section tells the reader that something is unknown when the chapter has in fact just settled it, which is the 'unknown because the manuscript has not yet done the work' category the book's own taxonomy is meant to exclude.
evidence: The chapter's own §3 arithmetic (12.8B active from top-2-of-8 plus always-on) and §4 Measurement item 3 (routing hyperparameter x parameters-per-expert gives active per token) already establish the deterministic relation; §7 restates it as settled and then lists it as open.
root_cause: The bullet was drafted as an open question before the deterministic relation was written into §3, and was not reconciled when §3 was completed.
correction: Move the settled statement into §3 or §4 as a positive fact ('under standard top-k routing the active parameter count per token is deterministic: k x params-per-expert + always-on; only variable-k, capacity dropping, or expert-unavailable fallback make it vary'), and rewrite the §7 bullet as the narrow open question it actually is: 'Under which implementations do variable-k, capacity dropping, or expert-unavailable fallback actually fire, and how much do they move the effective active count?'
acceptance_test: Every bullet in a 'What We Still Don't Know' section states a question the chapter has not already answered; no bullet's own body contains its resolution.

page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Concept' — 'KV cache as a concept' subsection (per-token figures and the 9.2K total); Ch 3 §3 'Why MoE saves compute but not KV cache memory' and Table 3-3 row 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit)'; Ch 4 canonical box row 'KV precision'
quoted_clause: It is on the order of **~256 KiB (0.26 MB) per token for a 7B-class model (32 layers, d_hidden 4096, full-MHA) and ~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB) per token for a 70B-class model (80 layers, d_hidden 8192, full-MHA)** at 8-bit precision. [...] At 9.2K tokens the raw byte-halving figure gives ~12.06 GB (not ~13.4 GB ...)
observed: The canonical scenario declares KV precision = FP16 (Ch 4 box: 'KV precision | FP16 (2.62 MB/token -> ~24.1 GB @ 9.2K input-only; ~24.9 GB @ 9.5K input+output'), and every capacity number in the book (24.1/24.9 GB per request, 436 GB KV budget, 17 slots, 6/21/9/32 hosts) is built on the FP16 figure. But the headline per-token KV number the reader meets first (Ch 1) is the 8-bit figure, and Ch 3's Table 3-3 states the canonical request's KV as '~12 GB' (8-bit) with no FP16 row. Two different per-request KV figures for the same canonical request (12.06 GB and 24.1 GB) circulate across three chapters, distinguished only by a precision tag the reader must carry. A reader who lifts '1.31 MB/token' from Ch 1 into a capacity calculation halves the canonical KV budget and doubles the concurrency ceiling.
evidence: Ch 1: 1.31 MB/token (8-bit) headline, with 2.62 MB/token (FP16) mentioned in the same paragraph. Ch 3 Table 3-3: 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit) | ~12 GB | ~0.6 GB' (FP16 values appear only in the prose: '~24 GB' and '~1.2 GB'). Ch 4: canonical KV precision FP16; all fleet arithmetic on 24.9 GB/request. Recomputed: 9,200 x 1.31072 MB = 12.06 GB; 9,200 x 2.62144 MB = 24.12 GB; 9,500 x 2.62144 MB = 24.90 GB.
root_cause: Ch 1 introduces the quantization variant as the illustrative headline because it is the more interesting number, while the canonical scenario's declared precision is FP16; the two were never reconciled at the point of first use.
correction: In Ch 1, lead with the canonical precision: 'at the canonical FP16 KV precision, ~2.62 MB/token for the 70B reference (2 x 80 x 8,192 x 2 B), i.e. ~24.1 GB for a 9.2K request; at 8-bit this halves to ~1.31 MB/token and ~12.06 GB'. In Ch 3 Table 3-3, add the FP16 row (dense ~24.1 GB, challenger ~1.2 GB) alongside the 8-bit row, or relabel the row 'at 8-bit KV (canonical FP16 values in the prose)'. Add one sentence in Ch 1 pointing forward: 'the canonical scenario's KV precision is FP16 (Ch 4); the 8-bit figures here are the quantization variant, not the canonical budget'.
acceptance_test: Every canonical per-request KV figure quoted anywhere in the book states its precision in the same line; the canonical request's KV budget (24.1/24.9 GB) is the first figure a reader meets, and the 8-bit variant is explicitly marked as a variant.

page_hint: Book-wide — figure captions for Fig 1.1, Fig 1.2, Fig 2.1, Fig 2.2, Fig 3.1, Fig 3.2, Fig 3.3, Fig 3.4, Fig 4.1
quoted_clause: Fig 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline, in two process bands plus the persistent KV cache. PREFILL (top) is the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt; it populates the persistent KV cache and is the dominant contributor to TTFT (time to first token — though TTFT also includes queueing, preprocessing, and transport, so model prefill latency is a component of, not identical to, user-observed TTFT). [...] Color is figure-local decoration — each box is titled. [...] [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
observed: Every figure caption in the chunk runs roughly 80–160 words and mixes four distinct jobs: (a) what the figure shows, (b) scope/caveat qualifications, (c) label and colour conventions, (d) cross-references to other figures and chapters. The result is that the caption — the only text a reader sees next to a figure — is longer and harder to parse than the figure it describes, and the reader's first line of orientation ('what should I learn from this?') is buried in the middle of a defensive paragraph. The 'Color is figure-local decoration — each box is titled; do not carry a color meaning from Fig 1.1 into this figure' disclaimer is repeated verbatim in at least two captions and belongs in a single front-matter note.
evidence: Caption lengths in the chunk: Fig 1.1 ~95 words; Fig 1.2 ~130 words; Fig 2.1 ~150 words; Fig 2.2 ~75 words; Fig 3.1 ~65 words; Fig 3.2 ~85 words; Fig 3.3 ~70 words; Fig 3.4 ~110 words; Fig 4.1 ~70 words. Each caption ends with a bracketed evidence label and several carry a second italic 'what to learn' line beneath the figure, so the reader encounters two prose blocks per figure.
root_cause: Captions were written as self-contained defence documents (each figure must survive being read out of context) rather than as reader-facing orientation, with no house rule separating 'what to learn' from 'scope caveats'.
correction: Adopt a two-tier caption convention and state it once in the front matter: (1) a bold one-sentence 'what to learn' line immediately under the figure (this is the line the reader should be able to quote); (2) a smaller 'Scope / caveats' line for qualifications, colour/label conventions, and cross-references. Move the repeated colour disclaimer into the front-matter figure-conventions note. Where the italic line under the figure already says what to learn, merge it into tier (1) rather than duplicating it.
acceptance_test: No figure caption exceeds ~45 words before any scope line; every figure has exactly one 'what to learn' sentence; the colour-convention disclaimer appears once in the book, not once per figure.

quoted_clause: Prefill FLOPs scale with input length; in decode, the weight-read bytes per token are fixed, so at a given HBM bandwidth the decode rate is roughly constant per token.
observed: The clause is about the weight-read component but is phrased as a statement about the decode rate, which contradicts the chapter's own §4 Measurement item 2 ('An increasing TPOT as the sequence lengthens reveals growing KV-attention cost' and 'TPOT does not have to stay constant'). A reader could carry away 'decode time per token is constant regardless of context length', which is the misconception the book elsewhere warns against.
evidence: Ch 2 §4 item 2 states the opposite emphasis; Ch 1 §1 'Attention' states 'the per-token step is a linear cost in context length'; Ch 2 §1 'Decode' states 'the attention term grows with context and is the one that eventually binds at long context'.
root_cause: A component-level statement was generalized to the whole step.
correction: Rewrite: 'in decode, the weight-read bytes per token are fixed, so the weight-streaming component of the step is constant per token; the attention component grows linearly with the cached sequence, so the observed TPOT can rise with context length — measure the curve rather than assuming either shape.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 2 asserts that decode time per token is constant in context length without naming the component it refers to.

quoted_clause: The full-attention component is *not* captured by $2NL$ — it grows ~quadratically with sequence length (Ch 22), so for a 9.2K-token prefill $2NL$ is a lower bound on total compute, not the whole story.
observed: The caveat is correct but unquantified, and at the canonical context length the omitted term is negligible. A reader who has just been told 'the lower bound already exceeds the H100 peak' may reasonably suspect the omitted attention term could change the verdict, and the book gives no basis for judging. Quantifying it removes a needless worry and strengthens the argument.
evidence: Recomputed for the canonical geometry (L = 9,200, d_model = 8,192, causal): attention FLOPs = 2 x L^2 x d_model = 2 x 8.464e7 x 8,192 = 1.39e12 FLOPs (1.39 TFLOP), i.e. ~0.11% of the 1.288 PFLOP 2NL figure (0.22% if the causal halving is not applied). The lower bound is therefore tight to within ~0.2% at 9.2K.
root_cause: The caveat was carried over from the general L^2 discussion without a canonical-scale check.
correction: Add one clause: 'at the canonical 9.2K context the omitted attention term is ~1.4 TFLOP, about 0.1% of 2NL, so the lower bound is tight here; the gap widens with context (Ch 22).'
acceptance_test: The reader can tell from the text whether the omitted attention term could change the canonical prefill verdict, and the answer is given numerically.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — Table 2-1 row 'Prefill: regime verdict'; Fig 2.2 caption; 'Worked example arithmetic details' prefill bullet
quoted_clause: | Prefill: regime verdict | compute-bound regime | arithmetic intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte > ridge ~295 -> on the compute-bound side of the roofline [canonical scenario][DERIVED] |
observed: The ~9.2K FLOP/byte figure is the single-request prefill intensity (one request's 9,200 tokens against one pass over the 140 GB of weights). At the canonical fleet operating point several prefills share a weight pass, so the intensity is B x 9.2K FLOP/byte — strictly further from the ridge. The book never says this, so the reader may take ~9.2K as the fleet's operating intensity and infer the compute-bound verdict is marginal (9.2K vs 295 is ~31x, so it is not marginal, but the margin is understated).
evidence: Recomputed: prefill weight-matmul FLOPs per GPU per step = 2 x 8.75e9 x (B x 9,200); weight bytes = 17.5 GB; AI = B x 9,200 FLOP/byte. At B = 2.1 (the canonical 17 slots / 8 GPUs) AI = ~19.3K FLOP/byte, i.e. ~65x the ridge.
root_cause: The intensity was computed for the single-request illustration and reused as the regime statement without noting the batching dependence.
correction: Add to the regime row or the prefill bullet: 'the ~9.2K FLOP/byte figure is the single-request intensity; with B concurrent prefills sharing the weight pass the intensity is B x 9.2K, so the compute-bound verdict strengthens with batching, not weakens.'
acceptance_test: The reader can state the prefill arithmetic intensity at the canonical concurrency and confirm it is further from the ridge than the single-request value.
